title: "Miles to Go Before We Sleep": Cutting Edge Treatments and Technologies in Sleep Health
speaker: Prof. Cathy Goldstein
speaker_title: M.D.; Professor of Neurology, Sleep Disorders Center
description: Prof. Goldstein will present the latest research findings on treating insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, and circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom. Sponsorship: University of Michigan Health Victors Care.
speaker_bio: Cathy Goldstein, M.D is Professor of Neurology at the University of Michigan Sleep Disorders Center, and faculty lead at UM’s Eisenberg Depression Center Mobile Technologies Core and the UM Mobile Technology Research Innovation Collaborative (MeTRIC). Professor Goldstein’s research uses sleep tracking devices and mathematical modeling to assess sleep patterns and circadian rhythms to determine their role in health and disease (including women’s reproductive health, multiple sclerosis, and gastrointestinal conditions). Her international expertise in sleep tracking technology is highlighted by her role as a lead author of the ‘State of the Science and Recommendations for Using Wearable Technology in Sleep and Circadian Research’ from the Sleep Research Society, and as a member of the task force on Consumer Sleep Tracker Guidelines of the World Sleep Society.

title: Presidential Power Unleashed: Trump, The Unitary Executive, and What Comes Next
speaker: Mitchel Sollenberger, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Professor of Political Science; Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education and Student Success
description: When a President proclaims that he may ‘do whatever he wants,’ one must ask: what becomes of the delicate balance that the Framers sought to establish? Political scientist Mitchel Sollenberger invites us to interrogate the core of American constitutional government by asking whether the doctrine of the unitary executive has shifted from interpretive theory into a partisan instrument of political power. In an era in which the presidency under Donald Trump is redefining the breadth of executive reach, the essential question is no longer simply what powers the President holds, but rather what meaningful powers remain for Congress, the courts, and, ultimately, the citizenry.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.
speaker_bio: Mitchel A. Sollenberger, Ph.D stands out as a scholar-administrator whose intellectual rigor and public spirit illuminate the contours of American constitutional order. As Professor of Political Science at UM-Dearborn and Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education and Student Success, he blends deep academic expertise with institutional leadership. His award-winning research—books like The Unitary Executive Theory: A Danger to Constitutional Government and The President’s Czars—and his prolific writings in top journals show unflinching clarity in confronting how executive power is expanding.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Biomedical Research and Technology: Creation, Development and Applications
title: Cyborgs: The Future is Now
speaker: Dr. Paul Cederna
speaker_title: Robert Oneal Professor of Plastic Surgery; Professor of Biomedical Engineering
institution: Michigan Medicine, Department of Plastic Surgery
description: It has been 40 years since Luke Skywalker received a prosthetic hand controlled by his peripheral nerves. Unfortunately, this peripheral nerve interface has not been achieved yet. Our UM research group has developed the regenerative peripheral nerve interface (RPNI), which amplifies the peripheral nerve signals and makes it possible to control an arm or leg naturally. In addition, the RPNI’s can be used as a peripheral nerve interface strategy to provide sensory feedback. In this presentation, Dr. Cederna will discuss the future of this exciting and innovative technology.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Paul S. Cederna, M.D., is the Robert Oneal Professor of Plastic Surgery and Professor in the Department of Biomedical Engineering at the University of Michigan. Academically, Dr. Cederna has authored over 425 manuscripts, published 31 chapters, and presented his work over 900 times at national and international meetings. He has been a Visiting Professor at National and International Universities over 70 times. He has won over 80 national and international research awards. Dr. Cederna has been the Chairman of the American Board of Plastic Surgery, Chairman of the Plastic Surgery Research Council, President of the American Society for Peripheral Nerve, and President for the Plastic Surgery Foundation. He is currently President of the American Association of Plastic Surgeons.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Biomedical Research and Technology: Creation, Development and Applications
title: Advances in Cancer Immunotherapy: How Can we Reprogram our Own Immune System to Fight Cancer
speaker: Prof. Maria Castro
speaker_title: Professor of Neurosurgery and Cell and Developmental Biology
description: Recent findings from the Castro-Lowenstein Team at the University of Michigan Medical School and the ongoing results of their clinical trial, which was recently completed at the University of Michigan, highlight the importance of harnessing the patient’s own immune system to elicit effective anti-cancer therapies. Recent exciting data related to immunotherapies and their use in treating incurable cancers will also be shared. Maria and Pedro have devoted more than two decades to pursuing the immune-mediated genetic treatment of cancer – medicine’s “ultimate frontier.” This gene-therapy strategy enables the human body to fight malignant brain cancer (and potentially other solid cancers) by employing genetically engineered viruses (vectors) to kill the tumor cells and elicit an anti-tumor immune response. Maria will also discuss the Phase I clinical trial at the University of Michigan and exciting developments that have revolutionized the treatment for lung cancer and melanoma.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Prof. Castro completed her PhD from the National University of La Plata, Argentina. And her post-doctoral training from the National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD. She is currently Professor of Neurosurgery and Cell and Developmental Biology, University of Michigan Medical School. Her program is developing immunotherapies that block brain tumor growth and recurrence, which led to an exciting Phase 1 trial (NCT01811992) for malignant gliomas, completed in 2023. A second trial for pediatric and young adult patients with recurrent brain tumors (UMCC 2024.064) has been approved by the FDA and will begin in 2025.

title: LAWLESS – A Critical Analysis of the U.S. Supreme Court
speaker: Prof. Leah Litman
speaker_title: Professor of Law
description: Prof. Litman will explain how the current Supreme Court is not ruling based on law, but instead based on vibes—the feelings of the justices and the political zeitgeist of the Republican Party. Among the worst of the bad vibes are the notion of conservative grievance and a commitment to minority rule. She will argue that the Court’s recent decisions reveal these influences, and how several cases the Court is currently hearing do as well.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Leah H. Litman, JD is a Professor of Law at University of Michigan, co-host and co-creator of the podcast “Strict Scrutiny,” about the Supreme Court, and author of the New York Times bestseller LAWLESS: How the Supreme Court Runs on Conservative Grievance, Fringe Theories, and Bad Vibes. She has received several awards for both teaching and research and scholarship.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Biomedical Research and Technology: Creation, Development and Applications
title: Groundbreaking Advancements in the Robert H. Bartlett Extracorporeal Life Support Laboratory
speaker: Prof. Joseph Potkay
speaker_title: Research Associate Professor in Surgery
institution: University of Michigan / VA Ann Arbor Healthcare System
description: Dr. Potkay’s presentation will cover groundbreaking advancements developed in or in collaboration with the Robert H. Bartlett Extracorporeal Life Support Laboratory. These advancements include the long-term support of living hearts outside the body, the development of an artificial placenta to support extremely premature infants, biomaterial development toward enabling life support without anticoagulation, and pioneering work in microfluidic artificial lungs and smart artificial lung systems.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Since receiving his PhD in electrical engineering from the University of Michigan under microsystems pioneer Ken Wise in 2006, Dr. Potkay has dedicated his career to harnessing the latest advancements in electronic circuits, microsystems, and microfluidics to advance medicine, with a strong focus on rehabilitation from lung disease. Dr. Potkay is currently a Research Associate Professor in Surgery at the University of Michigan and a Research Biomedical Engineer at the VA Ann Arbor Healthcare System. He is Head of Biomedical Engineering for the Robert H. Bartlett Extracorporeal Life Support Laboratory at the University of Michigan. His artificial lung research has been continually funded through VA and NIH awards since 2007 and has received international attention and news coverage, including at the highest levels of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Biomedical Research and Technology: Creation, Development and Applications
title: The Weil Institute and the Commercialization of Critical Care Technology
speaker: Dr. Kevin Ward
speaker_title: Professor of Emergency Medicine and Biomedical Engineering; Executive Director, Max Harry Weil Institute for Critical Care Research and Innovation
description: Death from critical illness and injury such as those from trauma, sepsis, traumatic brain injury, cardiac arrest and others exceed that of cancer and heart disease. Due to the complexity of these diseases, little progress has been made in developing technologies that could improve outcomes. The Weil Institute is a transdisciplinary research enterprise composed of clinicians, basic scientists, and engineers dedicated to researching solutions combined with entrepreneurship that accelerate the potential for moving new discoveries to the bedside. Examples of successes, failures, and barriers will be presented and discussed.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Dr. Ward is Professor of Emergency Medicine and Biomedical Engineering and the Executive Director of the Max Harry Weil Institute for Critical Care Research and Innovation at the University of Michigan.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Biomedical Research and Technology: Creation, Development and Applications
title: Tiny Bubbles: Harnessing Their Power in Medicine
speaker: Prof. J. Brian Fowlkes
speaker_title: Professor, Radiology and Biomedical Engineering
description: When we think of tiny bubbles like those in a glass of beer, we might never expect the power such a small object could produce given the right conditions. From the erosion of ship propellers to industrial cleaning to breaking of kidney stones and liquification of tissue, we will explore a few of the many ways bubbles can be used to affect their surroundings and be engineered to provide diagnostic and therapeutic tools in medicine.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Dr. Fowlkes conducts research on diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound including quantitative imaging such as volumetric blood flow for OB/GYN and traumatic brain injury and bubble production for drug release and high intensity ultrasound including histotripsy. He is a Fellow of the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine, the American Institute of Medical and Biomedical Engineering, the Acoustical Society of America, the American Association of Physicists in Medicine and the Institute for Electrical and Electronics Engineers.

title: Did State-Socialism Really Fail?
speaker: Brian Porter-Szűcs, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Arthur F. Thurnau Professor of History
description: Though it’s become a truism that the economic system of the USSR and its allies failed, the actual record is more nuanced. State socialism did not bring the grand achievements that its founders had hoped for, but neither did it leave these countries worse off than they were beforehand. In fact, most Soviet countries did better overall under socialism than under capitalism. Once we recognize this, we face a puzzle: Why did so many economists within the Soviet Bloc come to believe that they were working within a catastrophically dysfunctional economic system? And why, when presented with a crisis in the late 1980s, were they so quick to embrace capitalism?
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Brian Porter-Szűcs, Ph.D. is Arthur F. Thurnau Professor of History at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor, and the History Department’s Director of Undergraduate Studies. He teaches classes on the history of the economy, the intellectual history of capitalism and socialism, the history of Roman Catholicism, and the history of Poland. Prof. Porter-Szucs has won many awards, including a Michigan Humanities Award, the John Dewey Award for Outstanding Teaching from UM’s College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, and an Excellence in Education Award from L.S.& A. He’s authored numerous journal articles and books, including Commodified Communism: Socialist Values and Capitalist Prices in the Polish People’s Republic, and Faith and Fatherland: Catholicism, Modernity, and Poland, both published by Oxford University Press.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
title: Moving Target: Photography Between Modern and Contemporary Art
speaker: Dr. Brendan Fay
speaker_title: Associate Professor of Art History, School of Art and Design
description: Photographs hang in museums, and art schools train photographers. It seems clear that photography has claimed a permanent place in art and art history—but the story is, in some ways, a recent one, unfolding during a period of radical changes in art itself. From the G.I. Bill to the present, this presentation traces photography’s winding path through a rapidly shifting era.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Brendan Fay is an associate professor of art history in the School of Art and Design at Eastern Michigan University. He is the author and curator of Photography as a Way of Life: Minor White, Aaron Siskind, and Harry Callahan, a book and exhibition about teaching, learning, and living photography in the postwar United States (forthcoming April 2026).

title: When Good Intentions Go Wrong: Campus Activism vs. Academic Freedom
speaker: Jeffrey Veidlinger, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Joseph Brodsky Collegiate Professor of History and Judaic Studies; inaugural director, Raoul Wallenberg Institute
description: When do the noblest intentions betray the very freedoms they endeavor to safeguard? In this interview, we will probe the tension between zeal and expression, between cause and constraint. Can activism that aspires to justice become a form of silence? Join us in exploring the paradox inherent in protecting vulnerable communities while preserving open scholarly discourse.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.
speaker_bio: Jeffrey Veidlinger, Ph.D., the inaugural director of the Raoul Wallenberg Institute at the University of Michigan, is a distinguished scholar whose work bridges history, culture, and human rights. As the Joseph Brodsky Collegiate Professor of History and Judaic Studies, he has authored acclaimed books such as In the Midst of Civilized Europe, which examines the pogroms of 1918–1921 and their role in the onset of the Holocaust.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
title: Piecing Together a Movement: Art Quilts and the Fabric of Change
speaker: Leslie C. Levy, JD
speaker_title: Ardis & Robert James Director
description: An introduction to the Art Quilt movement, including the visionary artists who created the genre, their individual styles and examples of their work, and how art quilts changed traditional notions of what constitutes a quilt.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. Speaker will be presenting on Zoom only.
speaker_bio: Leslie C. Levy was named the Ardis & Robert James director at the International Quilt Museum in 2014. After earning her Juris Doctor from the University of Nebraska’s College of Law, Ms. Levy worked in both private and public services, including two international non-profits and 12 years as the Chief of the Consumer Protection & Antitrust Division for the Nebraska Department of Justice.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
title: Michigan’s Mystery Relics: Fact or Fraud?
speaker: Prof. Lisa C. Young
speaker_title: Teaching Professor in Anthropology
description: Over a century ago, tablets with ancient writing were discovered in Michigan. Some argued they were relics of a lost civilization, while experts identified them as fake artifacts. Interest in these relics continues to this day. This lecture explores questions about the evidence used to identify the authenticity of ancient artifacts, why these relics continue to intrigue people, and the ramifications of archaeological frauds.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Lisa C. Young is a Teaching Professor in anthropology at the University of Michigan. Her archaeological research examines changes in community organization and foodways of small-scale farming communities in the American Southwest. She also researches the histories of museum collections to explore the changing relationships between anthropologists, museums, and communities of origin. Public outreach and community engagement with diverse stakeholders, including Indigenous communities, are an integral part of her work.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
title: “Tell Me What You Eat”: Literary Perspectives on Food and Culture
speaker: Prof. Supriya M. Nair
speaker_title: Professor, Department of English Language and Literature
description: “One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well," notes the narrator in Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. Amidst an increasing focus on gut health, sustainable food systems, food sovereignty, food (in)security, and other social (and social media) topics, the place of food in literature and culture has come in for renewed interest in scholarship that goes beyond the gustatory text. How do a range of literary forms (fiction, nonfiction, cookbooks) and visual media help us imagine the significant ways in which food relates to our lived experience? If food has power, as Anthony Bourdain insists in Kitchen Confidential, how does literature reveal its power?
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Supriya M. Nair is a Professor in the Department of English Language and Literature at the University of Michigan-Ann Arbor. She is the author of two monographs, Caliban’s Curse: George Lamming and the Revisioning of History and Pathologies of Paradise: Caribbean Detours. She is also co-editor of Postcolonialisms: An Anthology of Cultural Theory and Criticism and editor of Teaching Anglophone Caribbean Literature. She regularly teaches courses on Food and Culture at the University of Michigan.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: Diverse Dimensions of Art
title: Screenwriting: The Hero’s Journey in 3 Acts
speaker: R. J. Fox
speaker_title: Writer, filmmaker, and teacher of English and film
description: The speaker will demonstrate how just about every movie – from Hollywood blockbuster or to small, indie film – follows the same story structure, divided by three acts and 12 steps along the “the Hero’s Journey.” In addition to providing examples of story structure in popular films, Fox will also touch upon screenplay formatting. There will also be an interactive component in which participants can explore these concepts through their favorite films.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: R.J. Fox is the award-winning writer of three published books, several short stories, plays, poems, a memoir, and 15 feature-length screenplays. He is also the writer/director/editor of several award-winning short films. He teaches English and film at Huron High School in Ann Arbor, MI. His movie Love & Vodka (based on his book of the same name) premiered at the 2024 Cinetopia Film festival.

title: What Does the Success of New Obesity Medications Tell Us about How Our Body Weight is Regulated?
speaker: Dr. Randy Seeley, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Henry K. Ransom Endowed Professor of Surgery
institution: University of Michigan School of Medicine
description: GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide and tirzepatide have revolutionized how we treat individuals with obesity. Should it also change how we think about body weight and how it is regulated? Dr. Seeley will discuss body weight regulation and how these drugs work to help individuals lose weight.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom. NOTE: the catalog's printed speaker line reads 'Prof. Ronald Suny' — an apparent misprint; the description and printed biography both identify Dr. Randy Seeley as the lecturer.
speaker_bio: Dr. Randy Seeley, Ph.D. is the Henry K. Ransom Endowed Professor of Surgery at the University of Michigan School of Medicine. He also serves as the director of the NIH-funded Michigan Nutrition Obesity Research Center (MNORC). His scientific work has focused on the gut-brain axis and its role in regulating energy balance and metabolism, emphasizing new treatment strategies for obesity and diabetes. Dr. Seeley has published over 400 peer-reviewed articles, and he has received numerous awards including the 2009 Outstanding Scientific Achievement Award from the American Diabetes Association.

title: Healing the Mind: Must We Accept Cognitive Decline? The Role of Psychedelics (Psilocybin) in Treatments
speaker: Omar Ahmed, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Associate Professor of Psychology, Neuroscience, and Biomedical Engineering
description: What if the path to healing the mind isn’t just about suppressing symptoms, but about rewiring the brain itself? Dr. Omar J. Ahmed’s research challenges conventional wisdom by demonstrating that psychedelics can induce lasting neuroplasticity, even in regions previously thought unaffected. His work invites us to reconsider: Could a single dose of a psychedelic compound be the key to unlocking long-term relief from Alzheimer’s, Dementia, Depression, and possible other cognitive disabilities, reshaping our understanding of mental health treatment?
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person only.
speaker_bio: Dr. Omar J. Ahmed is an Associate Professor at the University of Michigan, specializing in Psychology, Neuroscience, and Biomedical Engineering. His lab, OmarLab, investigates how neural circuits, particularly in the retrosplenial cortex, encode space, time, and speed.

title: Digital Privacy in the Age of AI: Risks and Protections
speaker: Prof. Florian Schaub
speaker_title: Associate Professor of Information and of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
description: Advances in Artificial Intelligence have led to innovations from AI chat-bots to smarter phones, cars, and homes. But with these developments also come new risks to your privacy: Is data about you used to assist or manipulate you? What if your private data is part of a data breach? How is AI used by cybercriminals to scam consumers? This talk will answer these questions, as well as discuss research advances that can lead to better privacy protections and policy, and what you can do now to protect yourself.
notes: $15 Member | $25 Non-Member. In-person and streamed live through Zoom.
speaker_bio: Dr. Florian Schaub is Associate Professor of Information and of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Michigan. His interdisciplinary research combines privacy, human-computer interaction, emerging technologies, and public policy. Dr. Schaub holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Ulm and was a postdoctoral fellow in Carnegie Mellon University’s School of Computer Science. His research has been honored with best paper awards at leading cybersecurity and human-computer interaction conferences. Dr. Schaub is an ACM Distinguished Member. His research has directly impacted industry practice and public policy.

title: Regulating Business in America: A Long-Term Perspective
speaker: Prof. William James (Jim) Adams
speaker_title: Arthur F. Thurnau Professor Emeritus, Professor Emeritus of Economics, and former Peterson Professor of Industrial Organization
description: Since the Civil War, the United States has experienced periodic waves of regulatory and deregulatory fervor. The pro-regulation tendency is associated with the Progressive agendas of the two Roosevelts (Teddy and Franklin), while the anti-regulation tendency is associated with the Supreme Courts of the late-nineteenth and late-twentieth centuries. Drawing on the regulation of business in different types of markets (labor markets, industrial markets, public utilities) and different types of regulatory institution (legislatures, administrative agencies), this lecture will explore the economic and legal ideas, as well as the economic realities, that shaped these turns in American regulatory history.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: Aetna.
speaker_bio: Dr. William James (Jim) Adams is Arthur F. Thurnau Professor Emeritus, Professor Emeritus of Economics, and the former Peterson Professor of Industrial Organization at the University of Michigan. His research has ranged broadly, from public policies toward business in the United States to economic integration in Europe. His monograph, Restructuring the French Economy: Government and the Rise of Market Competition since World War II, has been called “one of the most penetrating [and] comprehensive analyses of French contemporary economic reality.” Adams has advised the Federal Trade Commission, the U.S. Ambassador to France, and several foreign policy departments of the U.S. government. He is a winner of a Golden Apple, awarded each year by students to the best teacher at the University of Michigan.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
title: How to Think About Midterm Elections Like an Expert
speaker: Dr. Eric Gonzalez Juenke
speaker_title: Professor, Department of Political Science
description: We will introduce the midterms as a crucial U.S. election institution that provides a check on power. We will look at how these elections can alter the direction and makeup of the federal and state governments. We will discuss what polls, campaigns and other information can tell us about what will happen on Election Day. We will discuss how different voting blocs may affect the election results, both in terms of turnout and vote choice.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.
speaker_bio: Dr. Eric Gonzalez Juenke is a Professor in the Department of Political Science at Michigan State University. He specializes in racial and ethnic politics, U.S. federal, state, and local elections, legislative representation, and immigration politics. His recent book The Presidency and Immigration Policy: Rhetoric and Reality examines how U.S. Presidents talk about immigration. His current research focuses on the election of racial and ethnic minority candidates to state legislative office in the United States.

title: The Pursuit of Happiness
speaker: Elizabeth Anderson, Ph.D.
speaker_title: MacArthur Fellow, Fellow of the British Academy, and John Dewey Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy and Women’s Studies
description: John Locke wrote that people possess the rights of life, liberty, and property. Jefferson took that idea and changed a single word. In the Declaration of Independence, property became the pursuit of happiness, a deliberate shift meant to protect people from arbitrary domination, not guarantee personal success. Elizabeth Anderson applies that principle to the modern workplace. A boss who controls your speech, movement, and livelihood without accountability exercises the same kind of unchecked authority Jefferson opposed. Anderson isn’t putting words in his mouth; she’s carrying his argument to its logical conclusion.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person only. Anderson also gave the January 2023 Gourdji lecture on the work ethic (see Fall 2022 / Winter-Spring 2023 editions).
speaker_bio: Elizabeth Anderson, Ph.D., is a MacArthur Fellow, Fellow of the British Academy, and John Dewey Distinguished University Professor of Philosophy and Women’s Studies at the University of Michigan. One of America’s leading public philosophers, she has spent four decades examining equality, democracy, workplace power, and the conditions necessary for human flourishing. Her work explores the enduring gap between America’s democratic ideals and lived reality.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
title: The Impact of Social Media on U.S. Elections
speaker: Prof. Yanna Krupnikov
speaker_title: Professor of Communication and Media
description: This presentation will focus on the role of social media – and other sources – in the way people understand campaigns and politics. In particular, the presentation will consider why people may turn to social media for information and the role of social media platforms in political expression. Ultimately, the presentation will consider what we gain and what we lose when we rely on social media for political information.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.
speaker_bio: Yanna Krupnikov is Professor of Communication and Media at the University of Michigan. Her research focuses on political communication and political expression. She is the co-author of books, Independent Politics (2016), The Other Divide (2022) and Partisan Hostility and American Democracy (2024). Her current work focuses on the role of the news in people’s everyday lives.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
title: Why Policymaking Success Leads to Electoral Failure
speaker: Matt Grossmann
speaker_title: Director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research and Professor of Political Science
description: Are policymakers rewarded in elections when they succeed in moving public policy in their ideological direction? Or do they face a thermostatic backlash, as citizens judge their policy moves as too hot or too cold? My analysis of Congressional election outcomes since 1948 adds information on Congressional policy actions to traditional election models emphasizing the surge and decline of presidential support and referendums based on presidential approval and the economy. I find that the electorate reacts against the ideological direction of policy, voting against parties that pushes policy further to the left or to the right in both midterm and presidential years. Even after accounting for policy and traditional explanations, however, there remains a large midterm penalty for the president’s party.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online. Sponsorship: United Health Care.
speaker_bio: Matt Grossmann is Director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research and Professor of Political Science at Michigan State University. He also serves as a Senior Fellow at the Niskanen Center and host of the Science of Politics podcast. He is an author of The Not-So-Special Interests, Artists of the Possible, Asymmetric Politics (with David Hopkins), Red State Blues, How Social Science Got Better, and Polarized by Degrees (also with David). He is co-owner of Hooked (a bookstore/cafe). His forthcoming book is Policymaking for Realists.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
title: Presidential Power and Democratic Resilience: Institutional Change and the 2026 Midterms
speaker: Dr. Mitchel A. Sollenberger
speaker_title: Professor of Political Science
description: Dr. Sollenberger examines how the expansion of presidential power is shaping American politics in ways that are increasingly visible in the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections. Focusing on key governing norms, he looks at how changes in government institutions, law enforcement, media, and election rules affect what citizens see, believe, and ultimately how they vote. The lecture considers what these developments mean for the role of midterm elections as a check on presidential power in contemporary American democracy.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.
speaker_bio: Dr. Mitchel A. Sollenberger is a Professor of political science at the University of Michigan–Dearborn and a former analyst at the Congressional Research Service. His research centers on presidential power, constitutional law, and executive authority. He is the author or coauthor of several books, including The President Shall Nominate, Executive Privilege, and The Unitary Executive Theory, as well as numerous scholarly articles examining the modern presidency and separation of powers.

title: America’s First Medical Experiments in the Wilds of Northern Michigan: A 19th Century Physician’s 33-Year Study of Digestion via a Fur Trader’s Abdominal Shotgun Wound
speaker: Prof. Joel D. Howell
speaker_title: Elizabeth Farrand Professor Emeritus, Departments of Internal Medicine and History
description: In 1822 the fur trader Alexis St. Martin suffered a shotgun wound on Mackinaw Island. He was attended by the physician William Beaumont. The blast left a hole in St. Martin’s abdomen, and for the next 33 years Beaumont did experiments through that opening. We will explore their travels together through the wilderness of the early republic, discuss how the experiments led to our current understanding of gastrointestinal physiology, and question the ethics of how Beaumont chose to experiment on St. Martin.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: UM Victors Care.
speaker_bio: Dr. Joel D. Howell is the Elizabeth Farrand Professor Emeritus in the University of Michigan Departments of Internal Medicine and History. He obtained his MD at the University of Chicago and his PhD in History and Sociology of Science from the University of Pennsylvania. His career has included clinical care and studying medical history, trying to understand why (and when) we came to believe so strongly in the value of science for guiding patient care. Author of many books and articles, Howell’s publications have appeared widely in medical and historical literature. His research has been supported both by federal grants and by foundations. His awards include the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Investigator Award in Health Policy Research and the Burroughs Wellcome Award in the History of Medicine. Prof. Howell is a Master of the American College of Physicians and Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: The 2026 Midterm Elections: Process, Policy and Consequences
title: The 2026 Midterms: What the Data Tells Us
speaker: Professor David Dulio
speaker_title: Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Director of the Center for Civic Engagement
description: Dulio will examine the most recent data about what to expect in the 2026 election cycle. He will also examine the major races in Michigan including the U.S. Senate contest and the race for governor.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person and online.
speaker_bio: Professor David Dulio is a Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Director of the Center for Civic Engagement at Oakland University. He teaches courses on campaigns and elections, Congress, political parties, and interest groups. Dulio has published sixteen books, with two of his most recent being Congress and Religion: The Intersection of Faith and Politics and Campaigns and Elections American Style: The Changing Landscape of Political Campaigns, and has written extensively on U.S. elections, campaign finance, and political consultants. He also served as an APSA Congressional Fellow in the U.S. House.

title: The Founders Warning: Did They Predict a Crisis?
speaker: Don Herzog, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Edson R. Sunderland Professor of Law and Professor of Political Science
description: James Madison famously observed, “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” His point was not cynicism, but a clear-eyed understanding of power, human nature, and the institutions required to preserve a republic. Two hundred and fifty years later, democratic institutions face mounting pressures that the Founders anticipated and sought to constrain. This conversation examines whether the challenges confronting American democracy today reflect the very vulnerabilities Madison warned could threaten the survival of self-government.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person only.
speaker_bio: Don Herzog, Ph.D., is the Edson R. Sunderland Professor of Law and Professor of Political Science at the University of Michigan. A graduate of Cornell University and Harvard University, he has spent more than four decades studying the foundations of democratic government, political authority, and constitutional order. An award-winning teacher and distinguished scholar, Herzog is the author of influential works on sovereignty, legitimacy, and republican government. His scholarship explores the enduring challenges the Founders recognized in preserving democratic self-government.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
title: The Arctic Region in the Context of European Geopolitics and Security
speaker: Dr. Gabriella Gricius
speaker_title: Associate Professor of Strategy
description: Although it may seem as though the Arctic has just entered the collective consciousness with renewed American interest in Greenland, the region has long been of importance for climate scientists, military planners, and naturally individuals living in the Arctic region itself. This presentation will provide an overview of the region’s importance, stretching from Alaska, to Europe, to Russia – showing how changes in European geopolitics and security have direct implications for the future of the region.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom.
speaker_bio: Dr. Gabriella Gricius is an Associate Professor of Strategy at the Norwegian Military Academy and a Fellow with the North American and Arctic Defense and Security Network (NAADSN). She is also a Senior Fellow at the Arctic Institute. She is currently working on a project covering Nordic security community formation and hybrid threats in the European Arctic region.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
title: Four Ages of the North: The Broad Contours of Arctic History
speaker: Dr. John McCannon
speaker_title: Historian of Russia and the polar regions
description: Often conceived of by outsiders as primordial and timeless, the Arctic in fact moves through history like any other region on earth. This presentation will examine key themes in Arctic history—both human and environmental—tracing change and continuity over four broad time periods: indigenous, colonial, industrial, and contemporary.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom. Bio lists only past academic posts (currently a guide and lecturer for Viking Cruises); current institution not stated.
speaker_bio: Dr. John McCannon is a historian of Russia and the polar regions. He was educated at Yale University (BA) and the University of Chicago (MA/PhD). He taught history for 30 years, most recently at the University of Saskatchewan and Southern New Hampshire University. His publications include Red Arctic (1998); A History of the Arctic (2012); and Nicholas Roerich: The Artist Who Would Be King (2022). He currently works as a guide and lecturer for Viking Cruises.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
title: The North American Arctic: Myths and Realities
speaker: Dr. Jennifer Spence
speaker_title: Director, Arctic Initiative, Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs
description: The North American Arctic — spanning Alaska, Northern Canada, and Greenland — is often portrayed through simplified narratives: a frozen wilderness, a geopolitical battleground, or a region of untapped opportunity. The realities are far more complex. This talk explores common myths, examining how climate change, Indigenous leadership, geopolitics, science, and economic pressures are reshaping the region. Drawing on current events and policy experience, the presentation offers a more grounded understanding of a rapidly changing Arctic.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom.
speaker_bio: Dr. Jennifer Spence is Director of Harvard’s Arctic Initiative at the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs. A specialist in Arctic governance and public policy, her work focuses on sustainable development, international cooperation, and the challenges facing Northern communities. She previously served as Executive Secretary of the Arctic Council’s Sustainable Development Working Group and has held senior roles with the Government of Canada.

title: The U.S. Midterm Elections: What Happened Last Week
speaker: Prof. Josh Pasek
speaker_title: Professor of Communication & Media and Political Science; Research Professor, Center for Political Studies (I.S.R.); core faculty, Michigan Institute for Data Science
description: The November 3rd, 2026, U.S. midterm elections at once serve as a test of American democracy, a referendum on the Trump presidency, a decision point for the future of the country, and an opportunity to assess how the parties are jockeying for and perhaps cheating in their desire to lead the nation in very different directions. This talk will examine what we know so far about what happened in 2026 and what those results are likely to portend.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Online only; printed "NOTE DATE CHANGE" — held Wednesday, November 11 (not the series' usual 2nd Tuesday), the week after the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. Sponsorship: DTE Energy.
speaker_bio: Dr. Josh Pasek is Professor of Communication & Media and Political Science, Research Professor at the Center for Political Studies at I.S.R., and core faculty at the Michigan Institute for Data Science at U. of M. His research explores how social media and psychological processes shape political attitudes, public opinion, and political behaviors. He also studies ways to improve the predictive accuracy of public opinion surveys. Prof. Pasek’s current research explores how political information might influence public opinion and voter decision-making and evaluates how use of online social networking sites such as Facebook and Twitter might be changing the political information environment. He is the author of two books about American elections, Words that Matter and Democracy Amid Crises. His work has been published in Public Opinion Quarterly, Political Communication, and Political Psychology, among other outlets.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
title: Environmental Changes in the Arctic: Local and Global Impacts
speaker: Professor George Kling
speaker_title: Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
description: Environmental changes are occurring rapidly throughout the Arctic region, including melting sea ice and glaciers, rising temperatures, loss of snow cover and absorption of solar heat, thawing permafrost and the release of greenhouse gases, and increases in severity of wildfires, precipitation, and storms. These changes and their interactions are disrupting the function of ecosystems as well as the livelihoods and cultures of resident populations. Additionally, the changes are now having impacts outside the Arctic and are altering global weather patterns and amplifying global warming.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented in-person at WCC; in-person and online.
speaker_bio: Professor George Kling is a Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of Michigan. A limnologist (the study of lakes) and Arctic researcher, he primarily studies ecosystem ecology and how water, nutrients, and greenhouse gases are transferred between land, surface waters, and the atmosphere. Professor Kling is a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and has received numerous awards for his research on the impact of climate change on aquatic ecosystems from the Arctic to the tropics.

title: Democracy in the Age of Algorithms
speaker: Ben Green, Ph.D.
speaker_title: Assistant Professor, School of Information and Ford School of Public Policy
description: Ben Green’s work sits at the intersection of technology, ethics, and democratic governance. As a scholar of government algorithms, he asks a deceptively simple question: when machines make decisions that affect people’s lives — in courtrooms, in city halls, in public institutions — who is actually in control? His research examines algorithmic fairness, the limits of human oversight, and what it means to regulate artificial intelligence in a democracy.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person only.
speaker_bio: Ben Green, Ph.D., is an Assistant Professor in the School of Information and the Ford School of Public Policy at the University of Michigan and a Faculty Associate at Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Trained as an applied mathematician, his research examines how algorithms and data-driven systems shape democratic institutions and public life. He is the author of The Smart Enough City, and his forthcoming MIT Press book, Algorithmic Realism, arrives this fall.

series_name: Thursday Lecture Series: What’s Happening in the Arctic—and Why Should We Care?
title: Russian Arctic Policy, Security Strategy and International Cooperation
speaker: Pavel Devyatkin
speaker_title: Non-resident Fellow
institution: Quincy Institute and The Arctic Institute
description: What are Russia’s policy objectives in Arctic security, governance and international cooperation? How does Moscow perceive the current situation of ‘low engagement’ with the West in the Arctic, the volatility around President Trump’s rhetoric on Greenland, and the Russia-China relationship in the region?
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. Speaker presented live on Zoom. Printed bio reads "has published Arctic militarization, ..." — an apparent missing "on", kept as printed. Followed by the ticketed Arctic Buffet Lunch (11:30 am - 1:30 pm, $20).
speaker_bio: Pavel Devyatkin, a non-resident fellow of both the Quincy Institute in Washington, D.C. and The Arctic Institute, has published Arctic militarization, nuclear weapons and arms control, great power competition and regional cooperation. His writing has been published by the U.S. Department of Defense, Strategic Analysis, Polar Journal, Italian Institute for International Political Studies, and other outlets. He provides consultations to academic institutions, diplomats and businesses on Arctic affairs. A graduate of the London School of Economics and University College London, Pavel is an American of Russian ancestry.

title: “Every Person for Themselves?” How Artificial Intelligence (AI) Will Reshape the American Economy and Impact the Quality of Life
speaker: Prof. Jerry Davis
speaker_title: Gilbert and Ruth Whitaker Professor of Business Administration and Professor of Sociology, Ross School of Business
description: Every national economy has a distinct character — a mix of laws, norms, and habits that shape which kinds of businesses flourish. America’s tilt is toward markets: Outsourcing over in-house production, contractors over employees. AI will amplify these tendencies, using algorithms to set wages, negotiate contracts, and price goods. Left unguided, the result is an atomized economy where everyone fends for themselves, thus negatively impacting the quality of life. But smart public policy can change that.
notes: $15 member | $25 non-member. In-person (Washtenaw Community College, Morris Lawrence Building, Towsley Auditorium) and online via Zoom. Sponsorship: Michigan Medicine-UM-Geriatrics Center. The Fall 2026 Gourdji series was planned by Bernard Banet, Ron Bogdasarian, Ron Frisch, Judy Gourdji, Frances Schultz, Katherine Woo and co-chairs Gerald Gardner and Marie Vitale.
speaker_bio: Dr. Jerry Davis is the Gilbert and Ruth Whitaker Professor of Business Administration and Professor of Sociology at the University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business. He has spent his career studying the corporation as a social and economic force — how finance reshaped America, why large corporations are vanishing, and how to tame corporate power. His six books include Managed by the Markets and The Vanishing American Corporation. His current work examines how AI is transforming economic organization. Prof. Davis has received many awards for his research and teaching, including the George R. Terry Book Award for “Outstanding Contribution to the Advancement of Management Knowledge,” the Award for Teaching Excellence, Ross Business School, and Fellow in the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University.
